newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenyan coffee seen not affected by IMF aid ruling.
newsitem.headline: Kenyan coffee seen not affected by IMF aid ruling.

text.p: The Coffee Board of Kenya (CBK) said on Monday the industry would not be affected by the ruling of the International Monetary Fund to cancel a huge loan under its soft-lending Enhanced Structural Adjustment Programme.

The IMF decision forced the government to tighten belts amid fears of long-term damage to the economy. Finance Minister Musalia Mudavadi said it had expected $215 million from the IMF and other donors in this financial year before the IMF halted the loan on Thursday in a row over corruption.

"I don't think it will affect the coffee industry a lot, the World Bank support to the small holder farmers will continue and so should the Stabex programme from the European Union," a senior coffee board official told Reuters.

But the official added that farmers would benefit from a sharp fall in the shilling rate versus the dollar -- blamed on investor jitters following the IMF decision last week -- because coffee auctions were denominated in dollar terms.

"Because we are selling the coffee at the auctions in dollars, it could be leading to a boom for the farmer, at least for those who are selling their coffee this week and the next few weeks the shilling rate should be quite good," he said.
The official, who declined to be named, said that the potential for a rise in inflation could affect the prices farmers would need to pay for inputs such as fertiliser and chemicals.
The World Bank said on Monday its support for the coffee sector would not be affected by the IMF decision.
"We are not withdrawing our support to the coffee sector because of the IMF decision, but if inflation goes up it could hurt the coffee industry," a World Bank official in Nairobi said.
The European Union, which is supporting Kenya's coffee industry through its farm-stabilising Stabex programme, said there was no risk of Kenya losing its support to that project.

"Regarding ongoing programmes which we already have agreed about with the government, they will be continued and we are not expecting to make any drastic decisions," John Simpson of the European Union (EU) office in Nairobi told Reuters.
World Bank and EU projects run into millions of dollars.
The Kenyan shilling suffered further losses versus the dollar and was under pressure to weaken further amid heavy dollar demand from nervous investors after the IMF decision.
The shilling opened at 61.50/63.50 and then moved to a range of 62/63.25 from Friday's closing rates of 60.50/61.50 against the dollar, according to prices posted by commercial banks.

The East African weekly said on Monday that $300-500 million held by foreign investors in "hot money" -- mainly government securities -- would be withdrawn at the first opportunity, fuelling pressure on the shilling.
